D.C. Code attachment is a 2026 web print of the official code site; navigation links (§§ 1-605.01, 1-605.03) and site publication metadata (Law 26-140, Act 26-357, Public Law 115-334) were not counted as citations.

Prompts were counted from each assignment's own prompt text (input.json 'prompt'); instruction.md for assignments 2-5 repeats earlier prompts and those repetitions were not counted again. Rubric fields were counted per criterion: authorities named in the criterion text and each authority in the source field. Justification fields quote the prompt and add no authority of their own; those quotations were not counted again.

The two scenario memoranda (comparator_discipline_cases.pdf; supplemental_comparator_disclosure.pdf) are record evidence; their citation in rubric source fields was not counted. Fictional-by-design records are the scenario adjudications (Final Notice, Award, PERB Opinion No. 1904) and scenario disciplinary case numbers.

The second census added 159 internal Chapter 16 cross-references and statutory short forms omitted initially. It did not independently rescan every original occurrence, so the overall census remains incomplete. Navigation metadata and non-authority record references remain excluded as described above.

All 436 supplemental source-reading assignments received retrieval attempts: 372 initially unread occurrences in three batches, plus 64 added by the second census. Row histories preserve the initial unattempted judgments and later actual reads. Remaining unverified sources include historical agency and Civil Service Commission decisions, personnel manuals, legislative materials, secondary works, unavailable reporter pinpoints, and an October 2019 D.C. Register notice; each affected row records the specific attempts and limits.

All initial and later problem proposals received independent second review. Proposed Dennison, Bowman and Cafferello defects based on auditor summary labels were rejected; the source-reading proposals and reasons for rejection remain visible. Bowman and Cafferello cited_for labels were corrected with their initial labels retained.

The Article 12 grievance reference conflicts with both real 2020–23 and 2023–26 agreements and current D.C. Code section 1-617.08(c), but arbitration under that article is shared across the fictional record. The citation discrepancy is not treated as a rubric defect or a reason to reject the scenario premise. No criterion was found to reward relying on that discrepancy.

citations.cited_for: MPD's arguments that the Award is contrary to law

first_check.explanation: Section 1-605.02(6) permits PERB to set aside an award 'on its face ... contrary to law and public policy' (conjunctive). Framing separate 'contrary-to-law' and 'public-policy' exceptions departs from the statutory wording, although the D.C. Court of Appeals itself discusses the 'contrary to ... public policy' limitation separately (MPD v. PERB, 901 A.2d at 789) and in FOP (973 A.2d at 179) declined to decide the conjunctive argument. The provision also governs PERB's review of arbitration awards; court review of PERB orders runs through § 1-617.13.
first_check.excerpt_read: § 1-605.02(6): "the award on its face is contrary to law and public policy"; FOP, 973 A.2d at 179: "FOP further contends that the CMPA authorizes PERB to reverse an arbitral award only if the award is contrary to both 'law and public policy' ... By raising this argument for the first time in its brief to this court".

second_check.explanation: The statutory text uses the conjunction “law and public policy” and defines PERB award-review authority. FOP permits a reasonable PERB construction and did not decide whether both prongs must be met because that objection was waived. The phrasing as separate exceptions is imprecise, but should not be treated as a decisive legal error without the case-law qualification.
second_check.excerpt_read: §1-605.02(6): award “on its face is contrary to law and public policy”; FOP, 973 A.2d at 179: conjunctive argument not preserved.

The case at the citation is right: the uploaded Douglas opinion carries MSPB-reporter pagination, 5 MSPB 313-346 (printed footers 313 through 346), and the Award pins 'Cf. Douglas, 5 M.S.P.R. at 306' for the 'tolerable limits of reasonableness' standard. In the upload, that standard sentence starts at the foot of printed p. 332 ('the Board's review of an agency-imposed penalty is essentially to assure that the agency did conscien-') and finishes at the top of p. 333 ('tiously consider the relevant factors and did strike a responsible balance within tolerable limits of reasonableness'). Four courts pin the same passage to 5 M.S.P.R. 306. Grafton (Fed. Cir.) gives '5 MSPB 313, 332, 5 M.S.P.R. 280, 306' for tolerable limits. Love v. D.C. OEA, 90 A.3d 412 (D.C. 2014), quotes the full sentence and cites 'Douglas, 5 M.S.P.R. at 306' (n.22). Kemp (Fed. Cir. 2006) uses 306 for 'not all factors pertinent', which is on upload p. 332. McNab (MSPB 2014) uses 306 for 'not to be evaluated mechanistically', which is on upload p. 333. So 5 M.S.P.R. 306 corresponds to upload pp. 332-333, not to p. 332 alone as Sol and the first check say. The Award's pin is the canonical pin for exactly the proposition it cites. The premise is false, and in its ordinary cite-check sense 'correspond' is false too, because the M.S.P.R. page does correspond to upload pp. 332-333. The strongest counter-reading is the one the reconciliation took: at the page-label level no upload page reads '306', so the statement is 'literally true', and a closed-universe solver cannot prove the mapping without outside sources. I considered VERIFIED_MINOR_DEFECT on that basis and rejected it. The closed universe itself signals the parallel pagination: the prompt labels the upload 'Douglas v. Veterans Administration, 5 M.S.P.R. 280 (1981)' even though its first printed page is 313, and other criteria in this dataset cite '5 M.S.P.R. 280, 305-06' to this same upload. The dataset therefore treats M.S.P.R. pins as mapping onto this document. A response that correctly reports the 306-to-332/333 correspondence contradicts the criterion's wording, so it is unlikely to earn the 30 points, while a response that calls a correct pin an error does earn them. citations.context: required 2 points

first_check.explanation: Section 1-605.02(6) permits PERB to set aside an award 'on its face ... contrary to law and public policy' (conjunctive). Framing separate 'contrary-to-law' and 'public-policy' exceptions departs from the statutory wording, although the D.C. Court of Appeals itself discusses the 'contrary to ... public policy' limitation separately (MPD v. PERB, 901 A.2d at 789) and in FOP (973 A.2d at 179) declined to decide the conjunctive argument. The provision also governs PERB's review of arbitration awards; court review of PERB orders runs through § 1-617.13.
first_check.excerpt_read: § 1-605.02(6): "the award on its face is contrary to law and public policy"; FOP, 973 A.2d at 179: "FOP further contends that the CMPA authorizes PERB to reverse an arbitral award only if the award is contrary to both 'law and public policy' ... By raising this argument for the first time in its brief to this court".

second_check.explanation: The statutory text uses the conjunction “law and public policy” and defines PERB award-review authority. FOP permits a reasonable PERB construction and did not decide whether both prongs must be met because that objection was waived. The phrasing as separate exceptions is imprecise, but should not be treated as a decisive legal error without the case-law qualification.
second_check.excerpt_read: §1-605.02(6): award “on its face is contrary to law and public policy”; FOP, 973 A.2d at 179: conjunctive argument not preserved.

second_check.explanation: I tried to overturn Sol's MISCHARACTERIZED and could not, but the finding needs a narrow scope. It is an external citation discrepancy, not a rubric defect. (1) What the dataset says. Final Notice PDF p.4, ¶27: 'Officer Braddock may grieve this action in accordance with Article 12 of the collective bargaining agreement between the Department and the Fraternal Order of Police/Metropolitan Police Department Labor Committee.' The notice is dated May 22, 2024, and the termination took effect June 21, 2024. The fictional Award (braddock_arbitration_award.pdf, PDF p.1, ¶1) states that the Union 'brought this grievance ... under Article 12 of the parties' collective bargaining agreement.' The Article 12 grievance route is therefore a premise shared across the fictional record, not a stray slip in one document. (2) The real agreements. I downloaded and read both official MPD/FOP agreements. The 2020–2023 agreement ('EFFECTIVE October 1, 2020 through September 30, 2023') prints at PDF p.12 'ARTICLE 12 / DISCIPLINE / [DELETED]'. The 2023–2026 agreement ('EFFECTIVE October 1, 2023 through September 30, 2026') prints at PDF p.12 'ARTICLE 12 / DISCIPLINE / [DELETED]'. In both, Article 19 (Grievance Procedure) covers only 'an allegation that there has been a violation, misapplication or misinterpretation of the terms of this Agreement'. Article 50 sets the durations. (3) Why the deletion is not a document quirk. D.C. Code § 1-617.08(c)(1)–(2), which I read on the Council's official code site, provides that '[a]ll matters pertaining to the discipline of sworn law enforcement personnel shall be retained by management and not be negotiable through bargaining' and applies to FOP/MPD agreements 'entered into ... after September 30, 2020, and to any collective bargaining agreements automatically renewed on or after September 30, 2020.' The gap between the 2020–23 agreement's expiry and approval of the 2023–26 agreement therefore does not revive a discipline article. (4) What the scenario mirrors. MPD v. PERB, 901 A.2d 784 (D.C. 2006), which I read by targeted search on CourtListener, involves a pre-2020 agreement whose Article 12, Section 6 governed discipline timing, with FOP arbitration of a discharge. The fictional notice reproduces that older structure. Conclusion: measured against the real agreements in force for a 2024 termination, 'Article 12' does not supply a grievance right, so the reference mischaracterizes the real external document. That is an adaptation or scenario assumption: the whole matter presupposes arbitration of the termination and PERB review of the award. It does not show the task is unanswerable, and no rubric criterion rests on it (see intent record). The row's fictional_by_design=false label is arguably an audit-label issue, since the notice is a fictional record document. The authority it names, however, is a real agreement, and that is what this status measures.

second_check.explanation: Sol's VERIFIED_MINOR_DEFECT is overturned. The only 'defect' Sol identified is that Cafferello does not directly address rebutting a disparity contention. That gap comes from the audit's cited_for label, which drops Douglas's signal. Douglas note 65 (printed 331, PDF p.19, read in the page image and text layer) first says agencies must put in the advance notice the factors they intend to rely on, citing 'Cf. Albert v. Chafee'. It then says that 'this does not require designation in the notices of all circumstances that could conceivably be relevant to the penalty; for example, if an appellant contends that a penalty exceeds that imposed upon other employees in like circumstances, the agency would remain free to present evidence to rebut such contention notwithstanding its failure to have recited such information in its advance or final notices. Cf. Cafferello v. Civil Service Commission, 625 F.2d 285, 288 (9th Cir. 1980).' I read Cafferello in the Caselaw Access Project scan, with reporter page labels. The case runs 285–289. At *288 the court states that '[i]t is undoubtedly improper for the agency to cite and rely on infractions not contained in the initial notice', citing Albert. It then holds that the supervisor 'did not remove Cafferello for any reason not stated in the charges' and that the examiner reasonably found he 'had only considered the whole person in determining appropriate punishment', so the action 'was based on the charges contained in the notice'. A 'Cf.' signal marks a proposition that is different but analogous. Cafferello's distinction between unnoticed charges, which are barred, and unnoticed penalty-relevant circumstances, which are permitted, is a sound analogy for Douglas's point that an agency may answer a disparity contention without having noticed the comparators. The name, volume, page, pin, court and year are correct. The supplied attachment's '•ommission' comes from a scan-margin clip ('Cafferello v. Civil Service' / ''ommission'), which matches the case-name OCR noise already disclosed for this attachment. The citation is accurate in the original, and the label error belongs to the audit. See the audit_metadata_correction. I did not treat the margin clip as a separate defect, because the reporter citation is fully legible.

See Albert v. Chafee ... Such, however, was not the case here. ... he did not remove Cafferello for any reason not stated in the charges. ... Major's clarified testimony showed that he had not improperly relied on new charges but had only considered the whole person in determining appropriate punishment ... we also conclude that the challenged disciplinary action was based on the charges contained in the notice to Cafferello.'

source_reading_attempts: Retrieved and read official Statutes at Large at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-78/pdf/STATUTE-78-Pg241.pdf.
Read official U.S. Reports 461 U.S. 761, which prints the embedded citation as 78 Stat. 259.

second_check.explanation: I confirm Sol's VERIFIED_MINOR_DEFECT. Grace's text at *761 (CourtListener's text of 461 U.S. 757, with star pagination) reads 'a bona fide seniority system protected by § 703(h) of the Civil Rights Act, 78 Stat. 259, 42 U. S. C. §2000e-2(h).' I read the official Statutes at Large print of Pub. L. 88-352, the same GovInfo document Sol used, kept in the audit's private source folder. Section 703 begins on 78 Stat. 255. Subsection (h) begins at the top of 78 Stat. 257 ('(h) Notwithstanding any other provision of this title, it shall not be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to apply different standards ... pursuant to a bona fide seniority or merit system...') and ends on that same page, before § 703(i) and (j) and § 704. Page 258 opens with the end of § 704(b), and § 705 (EEOC) begins further down that page. Page 259 is the middle of § 705(g), the Commission's powers (technical assistance, conciliation, technical studies), and contains nothing from § 703. Statute-page pins in Supreme Court practice point either to the page where the cited provision begins or to the page range it occupies. Because § 703(h) begins and ends on 257, both conventions give 78 Stat. 257, and neither supports 259. Teamsters, the case Grace cites in the same discussion, cites Title VII at 78 Stat. 253, the first page of the title, consistent with this pagination. The error is harmless: the section number, the U.S.C. parallel (42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(h)), and the proposition (protection of bona fide seniority systems) are all correct, so any reader is led to the right provision. The defect is embedded in an authentic Supreme Court opinion supplied as an attachment. It is not a rubric defect.

(a) There is hereby created a Commission...'; 78 Stat. 259 opens '(3) to furnish to persons subject to this title such technical assistance...'. Grace at *761: '§ 703(h) of the Civil Rights Act, 78 Stat. 259, 42 U. S. C. §2000e-2(h).'

(1) The first check rests on misreading our own audit metadata. Sol read the row's 'cited_for: Same' as carrying over a retroactivity point. In this audit's row order, the label immediately before pd-0580 is pd-0579 (Franks, 424 U.S. 778-779), whose cited_for is 'Judicial alteration of seniority provisions'. Grace footnote 9, which I read in CourtListener's text of 461 U.S. 757, reads: 'Neither do we decide whether such an award could be enforced in the face of a valid judicial alteration of seniority provisions, pursuant to Franks v. Bowman Transportation Co., 424 U.S. 747, 778-779 (1976), to provide relief to discriminatees under Title VII or other law. See Dennison v. The name, volume, first page, court and year all match: Ninth Circuit, No. 80-5061, decided Oct. 5, 1981, Canby, J. (3) The pin covers the material. I used the Caselaw Access Project scan of 658 F.2d, which carries reporter page labels. The case runs 694-696. Page *695 begins in the first sentence of the opinion ('...summary judgment to the Department and [*695] Dennison'), and *696 begins mid-paragraph ('the present [*696] action indirectly seeks to confer the benefits of promotion on others'). Pages 695-696 therefore hold essentially the whole opinion: the Title VII consent decree giving 50% of promotions to minority class members; the holding that non-minority employees' compensation suit is an impermissible collateral attack; the reasoning that such relief 'would impose conflicting or inconsistent obligations on the Department' and would undercut Title VII's policy of promoting settlements; and the holding that the union had a chance to intervene. new_problem_second_review_coverage.direct_dcca_premise: D.C. Code § 1-617.13(c), read verbatim this session, provides that a person aggrieved by a final PERB order 'may obtain review of such order in the Superior Court of the District of Columbia by filing a request within 30 days after the final order has been issued.' The uploaded FOP opinion shows that posture: PERB, then Superior Court, then a DCCA appeal ('After the Superior Court affirmed the PERB's decision, FOP timely appealed to this court'). The DCCA then reviews the PERB decision as if heard initially there, and FOP n.8 cites § 1-617.13(c). The PERB Braddock decision is dated November 6, 2025, and the scenario date is March 2, 2026. The record shows no Superior Court filing or service date. On the face of the record, then, a direct DCCA petition is not the statutory first-instance route, and the 30-day window counted from issuance appears to have run unless a filing exists outside the record. I did not check how Superior Court agency-review rules compute the period or whether any tolling applies. These points concern the scenario premise, not a finding that assignment-5 criterion_1 (+4, 'should petition the DCCA for review') is a rubric error. The prompts instruct the solver to assume a DCCA challenge, and whether that assumption should be honored or flagged is left to reconciliation.

Register addendum were itemized; Chapter 16's internal cross-references to its own sections (for example '§ 1618', '§§ 1626 through 1637') and the DPM 'Active Issuances' list were not itemized.

Justification fields quote the prompt and add no authority of their own; those quotations were not counted again.

Fictional-by-design records are the scenario adjudications (Final Notice, Award, PERB Opinion No. 1904) and scenario disciplinary case numbers.

Coverage of embedded citations is a census, not full verification: of the citations inside the five real opinions and the regulation, those marked UNABLE_TO_VERIFY were resolved for existence only (CourtListener citation lookup or the citator links in the official opinion text) or not retrieved at all (legislative history, Federal Register, executive orders, Comptroller General decisions, unpublished Civil Service Commission and early MSPB decisions, the Federal Personnel Manual, treatises and law reviews, 1980 versions of Title 5). Their pin cites and propositions were not read.

Code); dcregs.dc.gov (official DCMR section documents); go.mpdconline.com (MPD General Order PER-120.21, eff. Nov. 27, 2022); Cornell LII for 5 U.S.C. § 5596.
